analysis.one_liner: Stops states from requiring food safety warnings or standards stricter than federal rules.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 283-139, but the Senate committee never acted on it, so no state food warning requirement was preempted.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred states and cities from setting food safety or warning requirements for food in interstate commerce unless they exactly matched federal rules. States could keep stricter warnings only by petitioning the federal health secretary for an exemption, or in a narrow imminent-health emergency. It would have wiped out laws like California's cancer-warning labels for food and state warnings on carbon monoxide-treated meat, replacing state-by-state protection with a single federal standard that, in many cases, does not exist.
analysis.who_benefits: Food and beverage manufacturers, packagers, and grocery retailers gain the most: one national standard instead of dozens of state warning and labeling rules means fewer labels to print, fewer state enforcement actions, and less exposure to state consumer-protection laws. Consumers get uniform labels, but uniform at the federal floor rather than the strictest state level.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits states from enforcing any food safety or warning requirement that is not identical to federal law, replacing a patchwork of state rules with one national standard.

States with stricter rules get only 180 days before their requirements lapse unless they win a federal exemption, and a state cannot enforce a policy the Secretary of Health and Human Services has considered and rejected.
Supporters argued uniform national standards end inconsistent warnings and compliance costs across 50 states.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers in states with tougher food warning laws, who would lose warnings their states judged necessary, such as cancer and reproductive-toxin notices under California's rules or state warnings on carbon monoxide-treated meat. State governments lose their main tool for protecting residents when the federal government sets no standard.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers relying on state warning laws

drawbacks.text: If the Food and Drug Administration has not set a rule on a food hazard, the bill leaves no warning at all: states cannot require one without a time-limited petition process, and they cannot adopt a policy the federal Secretary has affirmatively rejected after public comment.

The exemption process puts the burden on states to prove an 'important public interest otherwise unprotected' and no undue burden on interstate commerce, so stricter state protections would likely disappear by default rather than by deliberate decision.

Supporters' strongest point: a patchwork of differing state warning rules raises food costs and confuses consumers, and the bill leaves untouched state rules on freshness dating, organic labeling, dietary supplements, and restaurant sanitation advisories.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The convenience of one national standard is real, but the design trades away state-level protection by default: where the federal government has no rule, the bill removes the warning instead of creating one, and it even lets the federal Secretary veto policies states have already adopted. The costs fall on consumers and states while the savings go to food companies, which is why state attorneys general and consumer groups fought it.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by a wide margin, but it was referred to the Senate health committee the next day and died there without a vote when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced in October 2005, the bill cleared the House Energy and Commerce Committee on a 30-18 vote and was reported on February 28, 2006.

On March 8, 2006, the House rejected 170-254 a motion to recommit that would have required warnings on meat, poultry, or fish treated with carbon monoxide, then passed the bill 283-139, with 212 of 230 Republicans and 71 of 201 Democrats in favor.

House amendments added carve-outs: states keep authority over dietary supplement labels and over warnings about mercury in fish and shellfish, and the bill takes effect only if the health secretary certifies it creates no new terrorism risk to the food supply.

The Senate received the bill on March 9, 2006, referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and it received no further action before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and state governments are better off because the bill died: state food warning requirements, including stricter cancer and toxin warnings and carbon monoxide-treated-meat disclosure, remain in force. Food manufacturers keep operating under the state-by-state rules they wanted erased.

sides.party_line_note: Passage looked bipartisan on the surface (283-139), but the split was sharp: 212 of 230 Republicans voted yes versus 71 of 201 Democrats, and the carbon monoxide motion failed with 169 Democrats in favor and zero Republicans.

industries.industry: Food and beverage manufacturers and packagers
industries.note: The bill would have replaced dozens of state warning and safety mandates with a single federal floor, cutting labeling and compliance costs and shielding products from stricter state rules. Its main effect for consumers is the removal of warnings in states that chose to require them.
The bill defined notification requirements broadly to cover posters, advertising, and in-store notices, so retailers would no longer face differing state disclosure rules across state lines.

industries.industry: State consumer protection and food safety agencies
industries.note: States would lose the power to set food warning standards stricter than federal rules, keeping only a petition process that requires federal approval to act.
